Estimate the parameters of a FINN model

Source: R/finn-class.R
fit.Rd

Estimates the parameters of a model built with finn() from forest inventory data. The model simulates every site from its initial trees through the years of env, the simulation is compared with the observed stand variables and demographic rates in data, and the parameters of all processes – the species parameters of the mechanistic equations (for a process built with createProcess(optimizeSpecies = TRUE)), their responses to the environment, and the weights of any neural-network process – are adjusted together, in one joint optimization, until the simulation matches the observations as well as it can. The processes are never calibrated one at a time: this joint calibration is what makes the estimated processes consistent with each other.

The defaults are robust in most cases. A first call needs data, env, init_cohort, patch_size and epochs; everything else can stay as it is. finn_data explains the input tables, finn_loss how the simulation is compared with the observations.

Usage

fit(
  model,
  data = NULL,
  env,
  disturbance = NULL,
  patches = 100L,
  patch_size = 0.1,
  init_cohort = NULL,
  epochs = 20L,
  lr = 0.01,
  batchsize = NULL,
  loss_family = c(dbh = "mse", ba = "mse", trees = "poisson", growth = "mse", mortality =
    "binomial", regeneration = "nbinom"),
  loss_aggregation = NULL,
  loss_resolution = c("site", "tree"),
  loss_weights = "auto",
  weight_scale = TRUE,
  loss_recruit = c("simulated", "observed"),
  tree_data = NULL,
  control = finnControl(),
  device = c("cpu", "gpu"),
  threads = NULL,
  update_step = 1L,
  start_time = 1L,
  plot_progress = TRUE,
  folder = NULL,
  checkpoints = 100L,
  shuffle = TRUE,
  record_gradients = FALSE,
  env_autoscale = TRUE,
  nonfinite = c("drop_term", "skip_step"),
  reanchor = FALSE,
  anchor_cohorts = NULL,
  anchor_mode = "replace",
  anchor_min_dbh = NULL,
  teacher_forcing = FALSE,
  rb_gradient = TRUE,
  trees_offset = 0.01,
  ...,
  loss = NULL
)

Arguments

model

(finn_class)
The model built by finn().

data

(data.frame)
The observations: one row per site, census year and species, with the columns siteID, year, species, dbh, ba, trees, growth, mort and reg; optionally period_length, n_at_risk and growth_n. NA marks a response that was not observed and is left out of the comparison. makeObsData() and resolveSiteIDs() build this table from a tree list. The columns, their units, missing values and incomplete series are explained in finn_data, with the bundled fia_obs_dt as the example.

env

(data.frame)
The environment of every site and simulated year: one row per siteID and year, plus one column per predictor (for the bundled FIA data temp and prec, annual mean temperature and precipitation; see fia_env_dt). The rows are the simulated time steps, so env must cover every year from the first step to the last observation; the predictors are in natural units and standardised internally (env_autoscale). See finn_data.

disturbance

(data.frame or NULL)
Optional disturbances: one row per siteID and year with the column intensity, the probability (0 to 1) that a patch of that site loses all its trees in that year. Must have the same sites and years as env. NULL (default): no disturbance. See finn_data.

patches

(integer(1))
Number of patches per site when the fit starts from bare ground (init_cohort = NULL). Ignored, with a warning when it differs, as soon as init_cohort is given: the patch count then comes from the initial cohorts.

patch_size

(numeric(1))
Area of one patch in ha. Default 0.1. Use the plot size of the inventory (the bundled FIA data: 0.06). A model that was fitted or simulated with another patch size before gives a warning.

init_cohort

(CohortMat)
The trees of every site at the first census, from makeInitCohorts(). NULL (default) starts every site from bare ground with patches empty patches (no stems). See finn_data.

epochs

(integer(1))
Number of passes over the data. Default 20; a real calibration takes hundreds, until the parameters stop moving. epochs = 0 runs the set-up only (data tensors, loss_baseline, loss_weights) and trains nothing.

lr

(numeric(1))
Learning rate, the size of a parameter step. Default 0.01. Lower it when the losses oscillate; see also finnControl() for a learning-rate schedule.

batchsize

(integer(1))
Number of sites simulated between two parameter updates. NULL (default) takes all sites at once. Smaller batches use less memory and update more often per epoch.

loss_family

(named character)
The likelihood each response is compared with: dbh and ba by squared error ("mse"), trees by a Poisson, growth by squared error, mortality by a binomial, recruitment (regeneration) by a negative binomial. The defaults are robust in most cases; name only what departs from them, e.g. c(trees = "nbinom"), or "none" to leave a response out. See finn_loss.

loss_aggregation

(named character or list)
How the simulated cohorts are summarised before they meet an observation: the default is the mean over cohorts for dbh, growth and mortality and the sum for ba, trees and regeneration, which matches the tables makeObsData() builds. The alternatives ("size_classes", "quantiles", "tree") are described in finn_loss.

loss_resolution

(character(1))
Whether growth and mortality are scored per site, year and species ("site", default) or per individual simulated tree ("tree", which needs tree_data with a cohortID column). See finn_loss.

loss_weights

("auto" or numeric(6))
The weight of each response in the sum of the six losses, in the order dbh, ba, trees, growth, mortality, regeneration. "auto" (default) makes the six comparable by dividing each by its intercept-only baseline, so no response drowns the others; a numeric vector then multiplies these balanced terms (c(1, 1, 1, 2, 1, 1) gives growth twice the weight). Before 0.2.0 the argument was called weights, which is still accepted with a warning. See finn_loss.

weight_scale

(logical(1) or character(1))
Whether a numeric loss_weights vector applies to the baseline-balanced losses (TRUE or "auto", default) or to the raw, unbalanced losses (FALSE or "raw", the meaning of weights before 0.2.0). See finn_loss.

loss_recruit

(character(1))
Where the recruits of the simulated stand come from during the fit. "simulated" (default): from the regeneration process, which is estimated with the rest. "observed": the observed recruitment (reg in data) is fed into the simulation, the regeneration process is frozen and left out of the loss, and growth and mortality are estimated on a stand that recruits what was observed – the first stage of a staged calibration, see recruitment. Before 0.2.0 the argument was called recruits, which is still accepted with a warning. See finn_loss.

tree_data

(data.frame or NULL)
Individual observed trees, one row per tree and census, only needed to score growth or mortality per tree (loss_aggregation = "tree" or loss_resolution = "tree"). Unlike data, which holds one row per site, year and species, it holds the trees themselves. Columns and the two per-tree routes: finn_loss and finn_data.

control

(finnControl)
Settings of the optimizer: the optimizer itself, a learning-rate schedule and its parameters, gradient clipping. The defaults of finnControl() are robust in most cases.

device

(character(1))
"cpu" (default) or "gpu"; "cuda" is accepted as a synonym for "gpu". Only NVIDIA cards are supported, and a card does not always pay: see the section on speed below.

threads

(integer(1) or NULL)
torch's intra-op thread count during the fit. NULL (the default) leaves torch's setting alone, including one made through OMP_NUM_THREADS or torch::torch_set_num_threads(). Extra threads rarely pay; threads = 1 is the considerate choice when several fits share a machine. The previous count is restored afterwards where torch allows it (OpenMP builds, e.g. Linux). torch's native backend (macOS) accepts one change per session, so there the session keeps the count fit() set, and a count fixed earlier in the session cannot be changed (fit() then says so).

update_step

(integer(1))
Every how many simulated years the gradient is cut (truncated backpropagation through time). Default 1: a loss sees the processes of its own year only. The parameters are updated once per batch, with the gradients of all cuts added up. A loss is only scored at a year that is a multiple of update_step, so an observation year off that grid is not scored, and fit() stops when none is on it. The simulated state runs on uncut. Larger values let the loss see a longer stretch of the trajectory at a higher cost and with fading gradients.

start_time

(integer(1))
Reserved for a burn-in: the simulated year from which observations are scored. In 0.2.0 it has no effect – every observation year in data is scored – and a value other than 1 gives a warning. Start env at the first year you want simulated and leave out of data what should not be scored; see finn_data.

plot_progress

(logical(1))
Draw the losses of every response per epoch while fitting, each as a fraction of its value in the first epoch. Default TRUE.

folder

(character(1) or NULL)
Folder in which the model is saved every checkpoints epochs (epoch_<n>model.pt, readable with torch::torch_load()). NULL (default): no checkpoints.

checkpoints

(integer(1))
Every how many epochs the parameters are recorded in model$param_history and, with folder, the model is saved. Default 100.

shuffle

(logical(1))
Draw the batches in a new random order every epoch. Default TRUE.

record_gradients

(logical(1))
Also record the gradients of every parameter at each checkpoint, in model$gradients. Default FALSE; the record can get large.

env_autoscale

(logical(1) or character)
How the predictors in env are standardised before they enter the processes. TRUE (default): every predictor to mean 0 and standard deviation 1. FALSE: as supplied. Or one entry per predictor (named, or in column order): "auto", "identity", "0to1" or a function f(x) returning list(center =, scale =), e.g. c(temp = "auto", management = "identity") to keep an ordinal predictor on its own scale. The constants are stored on the model (model$env_scaling) and re-applied by predict()/simulateForest(), so env is always passed in natural units. See finn_data.

nonfinite

(character(1))
What happens when one of the six loss terms is not finite at a scored timestep (an overflowing likelihood, a target outside the family's support). "drop_term" (default) leaves only that term out of the timestep's gradient and reported loss; the other responses are still backpropagated there, and the occurrences are counted per response in model$nonfinite_counts and summarised in a warning when the fit ends. "skip_step" discards the WHOLE timestep – none of the six terms is backpropagated or reported there – which is what every version before drop_term existed did; use it to reproduce such a fit. The difference only shows once a term overflows: with finite losses the two are identical.

reanchor

(logical(1))
Fit by multiple shooting instead of single shooting. With the default FALSE the cohort state is initialised once from init_cohort and then runs free over the whole horizon, so simulation error compounds across every observation. With TRUE the simulated state is discarded at every timestep for which anchor_cohorts supplies an observed tree list and rebuilt from it, after that timestep's loss has been backpropagated – drift is then bounded by one inter-census segment. This is not the same as the gradient truncation controlled by update_step, which cuts the gradient but keeps the state; set update_step to the segment length to let the gradient span the whole segment.

anchor_cohorts

(list())
Named list of CohortMat objects, the observed state to restart from. Names are the simulation timesteps to re-anchor at (integers as characters, and entries of the model's internal year_sequence, i.e. timesteps that carry an observation). Every anchor must have the same number of species, sites and patches as init_cohort; the number of cohorts may differ between anchors and from init_cohort. The last observation year needs no anchor – nothing is simulated after it – and an anchor may not fall inside another observation's period_length window, because the aggregated rates would then mix pre- and post-anchor state. fit() copies the anchors onto its own device and never modifies them, so one list can be reused across fits. Ignored unless reanchor = TRUE.

Build the arrays directly – CohortMat(dbh = , trees = , species = , dims = , sp = ) – rather than via CohortMat(obs_df = ). The obs_df path runs obsDF2arrays(), which rounds trees to whole stems and silently renumbers any siteID/patchID that is not a complete 1:n sequence; on a simulated or partly empty stand that corrupts the anchor, and a renumbered site no longer aligns with init_cohort.

anchor_mode

(character(1))
What an anchor does to the simulated state. "replace" (default) overwrites it wholesale. "merge" keeps the simulated cohorts with dbh < anchor_min_dbh and concatenates them with the full anchor. Use "merge" whenever the inventory has a minimum-dbh threshold (FIA: 12.7 cm): an anchor built from it contains no small trees, so "replace" deletes FINN's entire regeneration pool at every census – on FIA that inflates 200-year equilibrium basal area by 41%. Nothing is double counted, because the observation is complete at and above the threshold. Ignored unless reanchor = TRUE.

anchor_min_dbh

(numeric(1))
The inventory's minimum-dbh threshold, in the units of the dbh column. Required by anchor_mode = "merge", ignored by "replace".

teacher_forcing

(logical(1))
Fit by direct estimation instead of by simulation, and never run a trajectory at all. The cohort state is reset at every timestep to the observed stand at the census that STARTS that timestep's observation interval – init_cohort for the first interval, then anchor_cohorts – so each year's demographic rates are evaluated at an observed state and the simulated state is never carried forward. The interval rates are then aggregated over the window and scored exactly as fit() already scores them, so growth, mortality and regeneration keep their usual meaning. The three STATE responses (dbh, ba, trees) leave the loss: predicting them requires a trajectory, and there is none here.

Mutually exclusive with reanchor, which is a different estimator: re-anchoring still free-runs the whole segment between two censuses and scores where it lands. update_step is inert under teacher forcing – there is no multi-year trajectory to truncate – and the anchor validation refuses any update_step that would change which observations are scored.

anchor_cohorts must supply an anchor for every observed timestep except the last (nothing is conditioned on the final census, because nothing follows it). Only fit() teacher-forces; predict()/simulateForest() always simulate, so a teacher-forced model is still validated by single shooting.

rb_gradient

(logical(1))
Take the gradient of the drawn death and recruitment counts through their expectation instead of through the draw. The stand still dies and recruits discretely, but the reparameterised draw and the rounding's surrogate no longer carry the sampler's noise into the gradient (on a national inventory most of the mortality gradient was draw noise without it). Default TRUE since 0.2.0; set FALSE to reproduce a fit made before that. The setting also decides which death draw the default createProcess(mortality_draw = "binomial") uses: the exact binomial with TRUE, the Gamma draw of earlier versions with FALSE (see createProcess()). It is stored on the model, so later simulations draw the same way as the last fit.

trees_offset

(numeric(1))
Offset added to the predicted stem count before the trees count likelihood, which is -Inf (poisson) or arbitrarily steep (nbinom) where a species' simulated count is exactly zero and the observed one is not. On the scale of the predicted count, so per patch. The default 0.01 keeps that cell's gradient comparable with every other term; the historical 1e-5 (poisson) and 0.001 (nbinom) left it at y/offset, four orders above the rest. NULL restores those two historical constants and so reproduces a fit made before 0.2.0.

...

Arguments of earlier versions, still accepted with a warning: weights (now loss_weights), recruits (now loss_recruit), and optimizer, lr_scheduler, lr_scheduler_params, clip_norm (now members of control = finnControl()). Any other named argument is passed on to the optimizer, as before; finnControl(...) is the place for it now.

loss

Deprecated name of loss_family, still accepted with a warning.

Value

The fitted model, invisibly. fit() trains the model in place, so the returned object is the one passed in, now carrying the training results (e.g. $history, $loss_weights, $loss_baseline, $param_history).

Details

What happens in a fit. Every epoch, fit() takes the sites in batches of batchsize, simulates each batch over the years of env starting from init_cohort, and at every year that has observations compares the simulated mean dbh, basal area, number of trees, growth, mortality and recruitment with the observed ones, response by response, through the likelihoods in loss_family. The six comparisons are added up into one number, the loss, and every parameter is moved a small step (lr) in the direction that lowers it. FINN is written in torch, so these directions (gradients) come from automatic differentiation; no knowledge of torch is needed. After epochs passes over the data the model holds the estimated parameters; fit() changes the model in place and also returns it. The per-response losses of every epoch are in model$history.

Rates over an observation interval. An inventory interval of period_length years is that many simulated years. The simulated yearly rates of those years are compounded into one rate per year before they meet the observation, with the same functional makeObsData() uses for the observed rate: growth as the geometric mean of 1 + g minus one, mortality as one minus the geometric mean of the yearly survival 1 - m; the recruits are summed and the stand variables are taken at the census year. A year in which a species has no trees in the simulation counts as growth 0 and survival 1, and the rate is spread over the full period_length, because the observed rate is derived from the counts over the whole interval. With finn(growth_rate = "period") growth is the compounded increment over the interval instead.

Reading the progress. With the default loss_weights = "auto" every response's loss is reported as a fraction of the loss a constant prediction (the mean of the observations) would get: 1 means no better than the mean, below 1 better. model$history holds these fractions, one vector per epoch in the order dbh, ba, trees, growth, mortality, regeneration (a seventh, unused entry is 0); the plot drawn with plot_progress = TRUE shows each of them relative to its value in the first epoch. A fit has converged when the parameters stop moving (model$param_history), not merely when the losses look flat; see the vignette Fitting FINN to FIA data.

Long simulated series. Taking the gradient through a long simulation is slow and the signal fades. fit() therefore cuts the gradient every update_step years; the gradients of the cuts are added up and the parameters are updated once per batch of sites. The simulated state itself runs on uncut. The default of one year is the fastest and the most short-sighted; larger values let a loss see further back at a higher cost.

Advanced estimators. reanchor restarts the simulated stand from the observed trees at every census (multiple shooting), teacher_forcing evaluates the rates on the observed stands and never simulates a trajectory, and loss_resolution/loss_aggregation = "tree" score single trees. They are for specific questions; the default single-shooting fit is what the vignettes use.

What makes a fit faster, and what does not

A fit is bound by the number of small tensor operations a simulated year issues, not by the arithmetic in them. So a GPU does not always pay (measure one configuration before committing a long fit to it), more threads rarely help (threads = 1 is usually fastest and the considerate setting on a shared machine), and several fits run side by side use a machine better than one fit given all of it. What does shorten a fit is fewer epochs: watch model$param_history and stop when the parameters settle instead of fixing a large epochs in advance.

Bounds on simulated mortality

Before the death draw, the simulation clamps the per-cohort mortality probability of every step to the interval createProcess(mortality_floor = 0.001, mortality_ceiling = 0.999) of the mortality process, so at least 0.1 % and at most 99.9 % of a cohort is at risk per simulated step however extreme the fitted rate. The bound is per step, not per year: on five-year steps the floor is 0.02 %/yr, on decadal ones 0.01 %/yr. Until 0.2.0 the interval was hard-coded to [0.01, 0.99], which made simulated low-mortality stands lose stems the observations did not. The per-tree mortality loss is not affected by either bound; it clamps at 1e-6. See createProcess().

The arguments that shape the loss, and how they combine

Ten arguments change what fit() optimises. They are not alternatives to one another: each sits on its own axis, and a fit picks one value on every axis. finn_loss carries the detail; this is the map.

axisargumentwhat it decidesdefault
which responses are scoredloss_family = c(<response> = "none")leaves that response out of the loss entirelyall six scored
which likelihoodloss_familythe distribution each response is compared withmse, mse, poisson, mse, binomial, nbinom
how the simulation is summarisedloss_aggregationwhat the cohorts are reduced to before they meet an observation: "mean", "sum", "size_classes", "quantiles", "tree"mean for dbh, growth, mortality; sum for ba, trees, regeneration
at what resolution growth and mortality are scoredloss_resolution"site": per site, year and species. "tree": per simulated cohort that started as an observed tree"site"
how the six terms are combinedloss_weights, weight_scale"auto" divides each term by its intercept-only baseline; a numeric vector then multiplies those balanced terms, or the raw ones under weight_scale = "raw""auto", "auto"
where the recruits come fromloss_recruit"observed" feeds the observed recruitment into the simulation, freezes the regeneration process and drops its loss term"simulated"
how the state is propagatedreanchor + anchor_cohorts, anchor_mode, anchor_min_dbh; teacher_forcingthe estimator – see the table belowsingle shooting
how far the gradient reachesupdate_steptruncated backpropagation through time: the gradient is cut every update_step years, the state is not1

The three estimators differ in how much of the trajectory each gradient sees, and therefore in what the fit is asked to get right:

state over the horizonscored responsesneeds
single shooting (default)initialised once, free-running to the end; error compounds across every censusall sixinit_cohort
multiple shooting (reanchor = TRUE)free-running within a census interval, rebuilt from the observed trees at each anchor after that step's lossall sixanchor_cohorts per observed timestep
direct estimation (teacher_forcing = TRUE)never carried forward: reset to the observed stand at every timestepgrowth, mortality, regeneration only – dbh, ba and trees leave the loss, because predicting them needs a trajectoryanchor_cohorts for every observed timestep but the last

update_step is a different axis from all three: it cuts the gradient but keeps the state, so under single shooting the stand still compounds while the parameters only see update_step years at a time. It is inert under teacher forcing, where there is no multi-year trajectory to truncate.

What cannot be combined:

  • reanchor and teacher_forcing – different estimators, not settings of one.

  • loss_aggregation = "tree" and loss_resolution = "tree" – the two per-tree routes score different objects (the observed tree at its measured diameter against the simulated cohort it became) and cannot run in one fit; finn_loss compares them side by side.

What a value silently implies: loss_recruit = "observed" removes the regeneration term, so a fit under it cannot be compared with one under "simulated" by its total loss; teacher_forcing = TRUE removes three more; and loss_weights = "auto" rescales whatever is left, so the total loss is only comparable between fits that score the same set of responses.

See also

finn_data for the input tables, finn_loss for how the simulation is compared with the observations, finnControl() for the optimizer settings, recruitment for the recruitment options (loss_recruit, the regeneration likelihood), simulateForest() to simulate with the fitted model

Examples

library(data.table)
# three Oregon FIA sites over two epochs; a real calibration runs hundreds
sites <- 1:3
Nsp   <- max(fia_obs_dt$species)
init  <- makeInitCohorts(fia_init_trees[siteID %in% sites], Nspecies = Nsp)
FINN.seed(1)
m <- finn(N_species = Nsp, recruits_dbh = 12.9,
          growth_process       = createProcess(~ temp + prec, growth),
          mortality_process    = createProcess(~ temp + prec, mortality),
          regeneration_process = createProcess(~ temp + prec, regeneration_capped))
fit(m, data = fia_obs_dt[siteID %in% sites], env = fia_env_dt[siteID %in% sites],
    init_cohort = init, epochs = 2L, patches = 4, patch_size = 0.06,
    plot_progress = FALSE)
#> ℹ weights: intercept-only baseline x your vector (dbh=0.00243, ba=12, trees=0.968, growth=1.84e+04, mortality=38.5, regeneration=0.768)
#> ℹ share of the objective at the intercept-only baseline (scaled): dbh=17%, ba=17%, trees=17%, growth=17%, mortality=17%, regeneration=17%

# the per-response losses over the epochs, and the baselines they were
# scaled by to make `loss_weights = "auto"` comparable across responses
tail(m$history, 2)
#> [[1]]
#> [1]  2.1722367  0.7110548  0.5395446 28.7657299  1.3195336  1.3620560  0.0000000
#> 
#> [[2]]
#> [1]  0.9194432  0.3529012  0.5377366 24.7921906  1.3246045  1.4133602  0.0000000
#> 
m$loss_baseline
#>          dbh           ba        trees       growth    mortality regeneration 
#> 4.117755e+02 8.303134e-02 1.033310e+00 5.429424e-05 2.596614e-02 1.302194e+00 

# give growth twice the weight of every other response, and lower the
# learning rate every 50 epochs
fit(m, data = fia_obs_dt[siteID %in% sites], env = fia_env_dt[siteID %in% sites],
    init_cohort = init, epochs = 2L, patches = 4, patch_size = 0.06,
    loss_weights = c(1, 1, 1, 2, 1, 1),
    control = finnControl(lr_scheduler = "step",
                          lr_scheduler_params = list(step_size = 50, gamma = 0.5)),
    plot_progress = FALSE)
#> ℹ weights: intercept-only baseline x your vector (dbh=0.00243, ba=12, trees=0.968, growth=1.84e+04, mortality=38.5, regeneration=0.77)
#> ℹ share of the objective at the intercept-only baseline (scaled): dbh=14%, ba=14%, trees=14%, growth=29%, mortality=14%, regeneration=14%
